cards.s: AWS setup & Docker
cards.html:
Chapter 5 · Level 3: Continuous Delivery to AWS. Now the pipeline stops being only a judge and becomes a delivery truck. Every merge to main builds a Docker image, pushes it to AWS without any stored password, deploys it to staging, tests it, and waits for your approval to go to production.

After this level you can:

  • Set up an AWS account safely: root MFA, an admin user via IAM Identity Center, budget alarms, region eu-central-1.
  • Write a production-quality Dockerfile for a Python service.
  • Authenticate GitHub Actions to AWS with OIDC and explain the trust policy line by line.
  • Deploy to ECS Express Mode (Fargate) with staging → production, manual approval, smoke tests and rollback.
  • Delete everything again so you are not billed.

cards.s: AWS setup & Docker
cards.html: What you build: deploy.yml: merge → image in ECR tagged with the git SHA → staging → smoke test → approval → production → smoke test; plus a one-click rollback workflow.

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html:
Watch out: Do this section before anything else

A new AWS account is a credit card connected to the internet. Leaked keys are found by bots within minutes and used for crypto mining. The four steps below take 30 minutes and prevent almost all horror stories.

1. Create the account at aws.amazon.com (you need a credit card and a phone). AWS changed its free tier in 2025: new accounts receive credits and choose between a free and a paid account plan. Read the current terms during sign-up; credits do not replace budget alarms.

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html: 2. Protect the root user. The e-mail address you signed up with is the root user: it can do everything, including closing the account. In the console: account menu → Security credentials → Assign MFA device. Use a passkey/security key or an authenticator app. Then stop using root for daily work, and never create access keys for it.

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html:
3. Create your everyday admin user with IAM Identity Center. Open IAM Identity Center (choose region eu-central-1, Frankfurt), click Enable. Then: Users → Add user (your name and e-mail) → Permission sets → Create → predefined AdministratorAccess → AWS accounts → select your account → Assign users → your user + the permission set. You get an e-mail with an AWS access portal URL. Log in there from now on, with MFA. On your laptop, install the AWS CLI v2 and connect it:

terminal:

aws configure sso          # asks for the portal URL and region
#   SSO start URL:  https://d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start
#   SSO region:     eu-central-1
#   profile name:   admin
export AWS_PROFILE=admin   # put this in your ~/.zshrc
aws sso login              # opens the browser; valid for some hours
aws sts get-caller-identity

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html:
The CLI now uses short-lived credentials that expire after a few hours. There is no long-lived access key on your laptop that could leak.

4. Budget alarms. Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget → Use a template → Monthly cost budget. Create one budget of 10 USD and a second of 25 USD, each sending e-mails at 80 % of the actual cost and at 100 % of the forecasted cost. Also enable Cost Anomaly Detection (same console, free), which mails you when spending jumps unexpectedly.

What if… the 10-dollar budget e-mail arrives?

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html:
What happens: "AWS Budgets: Monthly 10 USD has exceeded your alert threshold". Budgets are an alarm, not a brake: AWS does not stop anything, and the cost data behind them is updated only a few times per day, so the real spend is already higher than the e-mail says.

What you do: Find the cause in this order. (1) Billing → Bills, expand by service and region: which service, where? (2) Cost Explorer, grouped by Usage type: for example EUC1-LoadBalancerUsage is an ALB in Frankfurt running by the hour, PublicIPv4:InUseAddress are public IPs. (3) Delete the resource; for this book, bash infra/cleanup.sh. (4) Check other regions: a service created by mistake in us-east-1 is invisible while the console shows Frankfurt.

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html:
What if… I lose the phone with my root MFA?

What you do: Register two MFA devices for root from the start (AWS allows several), for example a hardware key plus an authenticator app, and keep one in a drawer. Without any device, AWS has a recovery process that verifies the root e-mail address and the account's phone number: it works, but takes time. Keep both up to date.

Concept: Why eu-central-1 (Frankfurt)

cards.s: AWS account setup: security and cost first
cards.html: A region is a set of AWS data centres in one place. Choose the one closest to your users and your legal requirements. For a German company, Frankfurt means low latency and data that stays in the EU, which simplifies GDPR discussions. Many AWS resources are regional: if you cannot find something in the console, check the region selector at the top right first.

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
A container image is a packaged file system with your code, the Python interpreter and every library, plus the command to start it. A container is a running instance of an image. Because the image contains everything, it runs the same on your laptop, in CI and on AWS. An image is built from a Dockerfile in layers; each instruction creates one, and unchanged layers are reused from cache.

Dockerfile:

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---------- stage 1: build the virtual environment ----------
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13 /uv /bin/uv
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 UV_LINK_MODE=copy UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never
WORKDIR /app
# Dependencies first: this layer is cached until uv.lock changes
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-install-project
# Then our own code (changes often, so it comes last)
COPY src ./src
RUN uv sync --locked --no-dev --no-editable

# ---------- stage 2: small runtime image ----------
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN useradd --create-home --uid 10001 app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/.venv /app/.venv
COPY models/ /app/models/
ENV PATH="/app/.venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    MODEL_PATH=/app/models/model.joblib
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD python -c \
  "import urllib.request as u; u.urlopen('http://localhost:8080/health')"
CMD ["uvicorn", "credit_api.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
What makes this Dockerfile production-quality:

  • Slim base image (lines 4, 16): python:3.12-slim is Debian with Python and little else. Smaller images download faster, start faster and contain fewer packages with security vulnerabilities.
  • Multi-stage build (Figure 11): stage 1 has uv and build tools; stage 2 receives only /app/.venv. Build tools never reach production.
  • Layer order for caching (lines 9–13): dependency files are copied and installed before the source code. Changing app.py reuses the expensive dependency layer; only uv.lock changes invalidate it.
  • --locked: the image contains exactly the versions in uv.lock, the same ones CI tested.
  • Non-root user (lines 17, 24): if an attacker breaks into the process, they are not root inside the container.

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
• Model baked in (line 20): the image is a complete, versioned unit. "Image :3f2a1c0" means exactly one code version and one model.
  • HEALTHCHECK and EXPOSE (lines 25–27): document the port and let Docker know if the app is healthy.

The .dockerignore file keeps the build context small and secret-free:

.dockerignore:

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
# Keep the build context small and free of secrets
.git
.github
.venv
**/__pycache__
.pytest_cache
.mypy_cache
.ruff_cache
.coverage
coverage.xml
mlruns
mlflow.db
tests
data
*.md
.env

Try it: Build and run locally

Install Docker Desktop (or Colima/OrbStack on macOS), then:

terminal:

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html:
uv run python -m credit_api.train          # creates models/model.joblib
docker build -t credit-api:dev .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e APP_VERSION=dev credit-api:dev
# in a second terminal:
curl localhost:8080/health
curl -X POST localhost:8080/predict -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"checking_status":"<0","duration":24,"credit_history":
  "existing paid","purpose":"new car","credit_amount":4000,
  "savings_status":"<100","employment":"1<=X<4","age":35}'

expected output:

{"status":"ok","version":"dev","model_version":"local-a7ad9a21934f",
 "data_sha256":"a7ad9a21934f"}
{"risk":"bad","probability_bad":0.6427,
 "model_version":"local-a7ad9a21934f"}

(Your probability and hashes will differ if you trained on other data. The container also prints one JSON log line per request; Chapter 7 explains them.)

Watch out: Apple Silicon and image architecture

cards.s: Docker for the app
cards.html: On an M-series Mac, docker build produces an arm64 image. Fargate runs x86_64 by default, where such an image fails to start with exec format error. In our pipeline the image is built on GitHub's ubuntu-latest (x86_64), so this does not happen. If you push from your laptop, build with --platform linux/amd64.

cards.s: When the container does not work: a debugging toolkit
cards.html:
CommandAnswers the question
docker logs <container> (-f to follow)What did the app print before it died?
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh credit-api:devWhat is actually in the image? (ls /app/models, whoami, env)
docker exec -it <container> shLook inside a running container.
docker inspect <container> --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}'Why did it stop? Exit code, killed for memory?
docker history credit-api:devWhich layer makes the image big?
docker run --memory 512m …Does it survive with the memory Fargate will give it?

What if… the container runs locally but the deployment never becomes healthy?

cards.s: When the container does not work: a debugging toolkit
cards.html:
What happens: The deploy step waits, then fails; ECS shows tasks starting and stopping in a loop, with Task failed ELB health checks.

Why: Work through the usual suspects:

  • The app listens on 127.0.0.1 (uvicorn's default!) instead of

0.0.0.0. Inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is reachable only from inside the container itself, so the load balancer can never connect (and neither can docker run -p on your laptop: curl gets Connection reset by peer). The bug hides when you only ever run uvicorn directly on your laptop, where 127.0.0.1 is fine. Our CMD passes --host 0.0.0.0 for exactly this reason.

cards.s: When the container does not work: a debugging toolkit
cards.html:
• Port mismatch: the app listens on 8000, the service expects 8080.
  • /health returns 503 because the model did not load (wrong

MODEL_PATH), which is exactly what our health check is designed to report.

  • Exit code 137 / OutOfMemoryError: Container killed due to memory usage: 512 MB is too little for the model plus pandas. Measure locally with docker run --memory 512m and raise memory.
  • exec format error: an arm64 image on x86_64 (box above).

What you do: Read the task's logs, not only the workflow's: CloudWatch Logs (ECS → service → Logs) or aws logs tail <log-group> --follow. The workflow only knows "unhealthy"; the container's own output says why.

What if… the Docker build fails with "/models/model.joblib": not found?

cards.s: When the container does not work: a debugging toolkit
cards.html:
What happens: COPY models/model.joblib … fails with failed to compute cache key: … "/models/model.joblib": not found.

Why: models/ is in .gitignore, so a fresh checkout has no model. Our deploy.yml trains the model before docker build (line 33); if someone removes or reorders that step, the file is missing. (The same error appears if .dockerignore excludes the path.)

What you do: Keep the train step before the build, and treat the error as useful: it proves the image can never ship without a model. In a registry-based setup, this step downloads @champion instead of training (Level 4).

What if… I need a secret during docker build (a private package index)?

cards.s: When the container does not work: a debugging toolkit
cards.html:
What happens: The tempting ARG PIP_TOKEN + --build-arg PIP_TOKEN=… works but stores the token in the image metadata and layers: anyone who can pull the image can read it with docker history.

What you do: Use a build secret, which is mounted only for one RUN and never stored: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token PIP_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/pip_token) uv sync …, built with docker build --secret id=pip_token,env=PIP_TOKEN .. Multi-stage builds help too: secrets used only in the builder stage never reach the runtime image.
